canonical_answers.title: Camshaft Chain Drive System — Inspection Process, Possible Defects & Correct Chain Tension
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Inspection process and possible defects that may be found (8)**

With the engine isolated and permit to work and enclosed space entry permit obtained, carry out the inspection as follows:

- The entire length of the chain should be checked, with close inspection of individual links.
- Check the chain for cracks on rollers, which might be caused by overloading or vibration; pitting on rollers may have been caused by deterioration of the lubricating oil.
- Check that the chain rollers can run freely and that the chain links can move freely on the pin and bushing (i.e. not "seized" between the pin and the bushing) — this might be caused by lack of lubrication.
- The tightness of the chain has to be checked. A slack chain will change the injection and exhaust valve timings, causing poor efficiency of the engine; if found slack, tightening should be done according to maker's instructions.
- Check for bright marks on the side plates and wheel sides — caused by misalignment of the chain.
- Inspect the lube oil jet nozzles for possible stoppages or deformations.
- Examine the rubber track of the guideways for cracks or other damage.
- Make a general inspection for loose bolts and screws, which might have been caused by insufficient tightening torque or excessive vibration.
- Check the teeth of the chain wheels; if abnormal wear is found, take measurement.

**(b) How correct chain tension is maintained, and the effects of incorrect tension (8)**

Correct chain tension is maintained by running the engine within limits — i.e. not overloading — and maintaining a routine inspection of the chain drive. The tension is checked by turning the engine with turning gear in the astern direction, so that the longest side of the chain is the slack side. After stopping the turning gear, the chain is pulled back and forth by hand, and the transverse movement should be between 1/2 and 1 link. If outside these limits, adjustment is carried out by tightening or slackening the adjustment nuts on the tensioner.

If the chain tightness is too high, there will be a high load on the chain wheel bearings, leading to early failure; excessive loading on the chain can also lead to excessive wear and damage to the chain links, rollers and sprocket wheel teeth.

If the chain is too slack, the timing of the fuel pump and exhaust valve will change, leading to poor efficiency of the engine. The chain will also vibrate, causing cyclic stress, excessive wear on the sprocket teeth, and can destroy the rubber liner guide bars.

canonical_answers.title: Load-Sensing Governor for an Alternator-Driven Auxiliary Diesel Engine — Description, Response to Load Increase & Droop
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Description of a load-sensing governor, with a sketch (8)**

**[Sketch]** Mechanical-hydraulic speed-sensing and electro-hydraulic load-sensing governor, labelled: Speeder spring, Ballhead, Centring spring, Needle valve, Receiving piston, H.P. oil supply, Speed pilot valve, Transmitting piston, Speed power valve, Increase-fuel output, Load computer, Load pilot valve, Solenoid, Load power piston.

The governor combines a mechanical-hydraulic speed-sensing element and an electro-hydraulic load-sensing element, and the two sensing elements are independent of each other. Since the load change is sensed prior to any speed change, the primary governing action is achieved by the load-sensing element; in this respect, the speed-sensing element can be considered both a fine-correction facility and a back-up system for the load-sensing element.

**(b) Action of the governor in response to a large increase in electrical load (4)**

During increased load, load sensing is achieved by an electronic computing circuit which controls a solenoid-operated pilot valve in direct proportion to the load change. The measured value may be either an electrical output from the generator or a signal from a torque-measuring circuit.

**(c) (i) The necessity for droop (2)**

Droop is necessary for parallel operation of the machines if stable operation is to be achieved. When two diesel engines are synchronised, either electrically or mechanically (geared), the speeds must obviously be constant with one another.

**(c) (ii) How droop is effected (2)**

As the load on the generator is increased from no load to full load, the actual speed of the engine tends to decrease (droop). To increase the power output in this mode, the engine speed setting is increased, and hence the fuel to the engine is increased.
